title: Chapter 9: Collections and Data-Structure Choice
description: Choose collections from a workload rather than habit. The learner compares list, set, map, queue, deque, hash, tree, and linked-order contracts; analyzes complexity and memory locality; connects HashMap correctness to equality; distinguishes immutable snapshots from unmodifiable views; and documents every ordering and ownership promise exposed to callers.

lessons.title: Collection, List, Set, Map, Queue, and Deque contracts

exercises.title: Collection, List, Set, Map, Queue, and Deque contracts: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Which abstraction associates one value with each unique key?
hints: Recall that Map is the abstraction with a one-to-one key-to-value association; List and Queue organize elements by position or processing order instead.

lessons.title: ArrayList, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, and memory locality

exercises.title: ArrayList, LinkedList, ArrayDeque, and memory locality: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why is repeated indexed traversal expensive for LinkedList?
choices: Each index lookup may traverse nodes
LinkedList stores its nodes contiguously, so indexing is just as fast as ArrayList
hints: Recall that LinkedList has no contiguous backing array; get(i) must walk node-to-node from an end, so an index-based loop over it can become quadratic.

lessons.title: HashMap and HashSet internals, equality, and collisions

exercises.title: HashMap and HashSet internals, equality, and collisions: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What resolves a hash collision between candidate keys?
choices: Assuming matching hashes imply identical keys
hints: Recall that hashing only narrows the search to one bucket of candidates; equality checking among those candidates is what confirms or rejects a true match.

exercises.title: TreeMap, TreeSet, LinkedHashMap, and ordering: concept check
hints: Recall that LinkedHashMap augments hashing with an internal linked list that records insertion order, unlike plain HashMap whose iteration order is unspecified.

lessons.title: Unmodifiable views, immutable snapshots, and defensive copies

exercises.title: Unmodifiable views, immutable snapshots, and defensive copies: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: After changing the source list, which result reflects it?
choices: An unmodifiable view backed by that list
Neither can ever reflect element changes
hints: Recall that Collections.unmodifiableList wraps the original list rather than copying it, so mutations made through the original reference are still visible through the view.

exercises.title: Collections and Data-Structure Choice: professional judgment
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A report must have deterministic insertion order. What is appropriate?
choices: Rely on the current HashMap order

exercises.title: Chapter 9 implementation lab: frequency
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `frequency`. Count how many strings equal target using case-sensitive content equality. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Array and its elements and target are non-null.
hints: Compare each array element against the target string with case-sensitive content equality and increment a counter only on an exact match.
Trace the public example plus a boundary such as an empty array and an entry that differs from the target only by letter case.

exercises.title: Comparator ties
exercises.instructionMarkdown: The `TreeSet` is ordered by a comparator that compares only `age`, so "Ada" and "Lin" — both 30 — are treated as the same set position and the second insert is silently dropped, leaving a size of `1` instead of `2`. Repair the comparator with a tie-breaker (for example, on name) so both distinct people are retained, keeping the demonstrated inserts, and explain why the tie-breaker fixes the count; do not replace it with a hard-coded print. Output tests verify the result; preserving the intended operation requires source review.
hints: Preserve distinct names when ages tie by adding a comparator tie-breaker.
